highlights: The draft Japanese Constitution, approved by SCAP and published on 6 March, vests sovereignty in the people, reduces the Emperor to a state symbol, and renounces war in Article 9.

Preparations for the 10 April general election, the first with women's suffrage, included party campaigning, voter education, Occupation Forces surveillance and non-interference directives, and broadened purge directives against wartime elites.

General MacArthur confirmed the Manila military commission's death sentence on General Tomoyuki Yamashita, while the courtroom and preparations for the International Military Tribunal for the Far East advanced in Tokyo.
The U.S. Education Mission headed by Dr. George D. Stoddard arrived to assist in reforming Japanese schooling, alongside compliance with the directive separating Shinto from the state.
Emergency currency conversion cut Bank of Japan note circulation from 61.8 billion yen to 15.2 billion yen, as authorities fought soaring inflation.
SCAP authorized the first post-war raw silk export, 3,000 bales shipped to New York to establish commodity credits for Japan.
The Labor Union Law took effect on 1 March and the tripartite Central Labor Relations Committee was inaugurated; mining labor standards were reinstated.
Japanese DDT dusting teams and mass smallpox vaccination fought typhus epidemics, and 180 companies were added to the Schedule of Restricted Concerns amid investigation of Zaibatsu war profits.

summary: Covering March 1946, this summation documents a critical transitional month in the early Allied occupation of Japan, marked by profound constitutional, political, and economic initiatives. Most notable is the publication of the SCAP-approved draft Constitution of Japan, featuring popular sovereignty, imperial demotion to a state symbol, and the Article 9 renunciation of war. In politics, intense campaigning and voter education unfolded ahead of the 10 April general election—the first featuring female suffrage—alongside rigorous surveillance by Occupation Forces and broadened purges of wartime elites. Economically, SCAP authorized the first post-war raw silk shipments to the United States to generate foreign credits, while Japanese authorities tackled soaring inflation through an emergency monetary conversion that drastically contracted Bank of Japan note circulation. The report also highlights the enforcement of the Labor Union Law, the investigation of zaibatsu war profits and indemnity claims, and aggressive public health measures deploying DDT dusting teams against typhus epidemics. For historians, this report provides exceptional primary documentation, including the full text of the draft constitution, pre-election campaign finance data, zaibatsu asset structures, and initial administrative preparations for the International Military Tribunal for the Far East.
